extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance history, Erasmus scholars, and those interested in Christian humanism and moral/religious criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive chapter from a scholarly biography of Erasmus discussing his writings (especially the Enchiridion), moral and rhetorical principles, and his attitudes toward princes, monks, war, and religious practice. Focus is on extracting the standards and prescriptions Erasmus advanced or the author's evaluative claims about him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of the Christian prince
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of the Christian prince is not to excel others in wealth, but, as far as possible, to seek the advantage of all. Turn not what belongs to the public to your own profit, but spend whatever is yours, even yourself, for the public good. The people owe much to you, but you owe everything to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Princes are 'vicegerents of the same Lord' as bishops and must render an account to Christ. They should consider the public good rather than personal indulgence; choose models for administration from Christ rather than military conquerors (Hannibal, Alexander, Cæsar, Pompey). Greater danger increases the need to avoid seeking indulgence for oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes violating princely majesty (læsae majestatis)
rubrics_metrics.description: He alone violates the majesty of the prince who, under the name of a prince, does things contrary to law, cruel, violent, or criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The usual clamour about offences against majesty should be a small matter compared with actual unlawful or cruel acts; personal attacks should not unduly move a wise ruler, who is a public person bound to the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles denote duties, not dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: Names like 'Apostolus,' 'Pastor,' 'Episcopus' are names of duties, not of government; 'Papa,' 'Abbas' are titles of love, not of dominion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office-holders should regard their positions as service and duty rather than as warrants for dominion or personal power; the rhetoric distinguishes function (service) from sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies against key vices and the simplicity of Christian law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Enchiridion closes with five chapters of remedies against lust, avarice, ambition, arrogance, and anger; these direct the conscience straight back to the sources of all Christian living, to the plain teaching of Jesus and the plain argument of common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction should be practical and simple: follow Scripture but do not take problematic biblical examples (e.g., Solomon's harem, Peter's denial) as excuses for immoral conduct. The Christian law is to be made plain to individual conscience, emphasizing inward responsibility over formal observance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate, measured critique intended to persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus guarded himself against direct assault upon established institutions; not the name 'monk' was a reproach, but the name 'bad monk.' He hoped to win the support of all classes by moderation and careful weighing and balancing of views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should target abuse and vice rather than assault institutions wholesale; rhetorical tone should be conciliatory enough to gather broad support for reform rather than provoke destructive conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission to compile a concise compendium of Christian doctrine and life
rubrics_metrics.description: A commission of pious and learned men should bring together into a compendium from the purest sources ... the whole philosophy of Christ, with as much simplicity as learning, as much brevity as clearness. What pertains to the faith should be treated in as few articles as possible; what belongs to life, also in few words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious teaching should be concise, clear, and accessible so that the yoke of Christ appears easy and pleasant; aim to make the essentials intelligible to all and avoid overwrought scholasticism that obscures practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection judged by motives rather than external form
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of Christ is in our motives, not in the form of our life, in our minds, not in dress or food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Christian perfection by inward intention and moral will rather than by outward practices, dress, or ascetic forms; external forms have dangers peculiar to each way of life and must not be confused with true piety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticize the vice, not the institution itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus had no quarrel with monks as such, but only in so far as they set more value upon forms than upon the true following of Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exposing abuses, make clear that the intent is to defend the institution's true purpose by highlighting particular faults (e.g., valuing forms over substance) rather than condemning the institution per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panegyric as a rhetorical device to reform rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: One can do more to help a prince by praising him for virtues he has not, than by blaming him for the faults he has; Augustine and Paul are cited as precedents for pious adulation used to reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may legitimately use idealizing praise strategically to encourage rulers toward better conduct; some rhetorical untruths in praise can be justified as instruments of moral improvement rather than mere flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace valued as the higher virtue for rulers over warlike glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus declares the absolute wickedness and folly of war; to govern the spirit, to control desire, to put a bridle upon greed, to restrain the temper—that kind of courage is peculiar to the wise and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise and cultivate peaceful virtues (self-control, restraint, public-minded governance), and treat warmaking and warlike exemplars with suspicion; the moral cost and waste of war make peace the more admirable aim for rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible, practical theological writing over scholastic quibbling
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus: 'I was not trying to train men for the prize-ring of the Sorbonne, but rather for the peace which belongs to the Christian.' There are too many commentaries and summas that obscure the art of living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theology and moral writing should be aimed at clear, practical instruction for living rather than complex scholastic disputation; avoid producing works that mix and re-mix old things into unreadable compilations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monastic ideal as voluntary, humble, laborious community
rubrics_metrics.description: True monks (Benedict and Bernard's ideal) were voluntary communities of friends, living in the liberty of the spirit according to the Gospel law, under necessary rules about dress and food; they hated riches, avoided offices, laboured with their hands, and dwelt in remote places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this ideal as a standard to critique contemporary monastic practice: value voluntary poverty, manual labor, avoidance of ecclesiastical office-seeking, and spiritual liberty rather than institutional privilege or accumulation of wealth.
